symptoms: Bleaching of spikelets, silver-white heads in fields, gray mold-like growth under high humidity.
Bleaching of individual spikelets or entire heads, orange or pinkish mass of fungal spores at base of glumes, shriveled chalky kernels.
Small, round, scattered orange-red pustules appearing primarily on the upper leaf surface and leaf sheaths.
Elongated, bright yellow-orange pustules arranged in linear, narrow rows or stripes parallel to the leaf veins.
Large, elongated, dark reddish-brown pustules on stems and leaf sheaths that tear the epidermis; matures into black lesions.
White to light gray, fluffy, cottony fungal colonies on the surfaces of lower leaves and stems, turning dull gray-brown with tiny black dots over time.
Irregular, elongated, speckled tan-to-brown lesions on leaves, speckled with numerous tiny, prominent black fruiting bodies (pycnidia).
Dark purple-brown to grayish-brown lens-shaped streaks and blotches starting at the glume tips, along with lens-shaped lesions on leaves.
Oval, tan-colored spots or lesions on leaves, typically featuring a tiny dark brown center point and surrounded by a yellow, chlorotic halo.
Normal spikelet head structures completely replaced by a loose, dark, olive-black powdery mass of fungal spores, leaving only the bare central rachis stem behind.
Infected kernels are wider, gray-green to dull brown, and filled with a black, powdery spore mass that emits a foul, rotting-fish odor when crushed.
Partial blackening of individual kernels, typically starting at the embryo end and extending along the groove, exhibiting a mild fishy odor.
Hard, elongated, dark-purple to black curved horn-like fungal structures (sclerotia) that completely replace individual grains in the head.
Premature ripening of the plant producing bleached, empty 'whiteheads', alongside severe blackening and rotting of the roots and lower crown stem tissue.
Superficial dark green, gray, or jet-black powdery mold growing across the surfaces of mature, standing wheat heads, often following wet pre-harvest weather.
Dark purple-black linear stripes or blotches on the glumes and water-soaked, dark green to brown streaks on leaves, often producing amber-colored bacterial exudate droplets.
Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that expand rapidly into large, irregular, grayish-green or light brown necrotic blighted lesions.
Dull brownish-black discoloration restricted to the base of the glumes, often visible on both the inner and outer surfaces of the spikelet shell.
Striking yellowing or reddening/purpling of leaf tips progressing downward, accompanied by severe plant stunting and reduced head emergence.
Discontinuous, light-green to bright-yellow parallel streaks or dashes running along leaf veins, creating a mottled mosaic pattern.
Crinkled, twisted leaves in early growth stages; normal kernels are replaced by small, hard, dark brown-to-black cockle galls containing thousands of dormant larvae.
Stunted, chlorotic plant growth above ground; root systems exhibit distinct swellings, knots, or small galls that inhibit water uptake.
Small, lens-shaped, white to pale-straw colored spots on leaf blades with a thin brown border, developing clusters of tiny dark brown fruiting bodies in the center.
Roots exhibit a distinct light pink to reddish-purple discoloration, followed by shriveling, dark brown rotting, and severe water stress symptoms in the leaves.
A faint pink to reddish coloration appearing across the glumes and internal kernels of developing green heads, without any visible fungal mycelium or spores.
Fluffy, dull-white fungal mats covering dead, water-soaked leaves immediately following spring snowmelt, forming hard, flat, irregular black sclerotia on the crown.
Fine, closely spaced yellow-white striations or dashes running parallel along the leaf veins, causing severe plant stunting and twisting of newly emerged leaves.
Small, irregular dark purple-brown spots on the glumes that dry into gray-tan lesions speckled with submerged, microscopic black pycnidia.
Light brown, water-soaked rotting of the coleoptile and primary roots, causing small, twisted seedlings that die shortly before or after emerging from the soil.
Elongated, water-soaked brown streaks on leaf blades that turn dark brown to black, developing a velvety, dark fungal layer under humid conditions.
Dark brown discolorations across the seed coat and embryo, causing poor germination rates and weak, stunted seedlings with dark lesions on their first leaves.
Patches of stunted, pale yellow plants; root systems are reduced, dark, and show swollen, dark, stubby root tips missing vital fine root hairs.
A powdery, soot-black mass of fungal spores coating the surface and cracks of harvested kernels kept in high-moisture, warm storage conditions.
A dusty, blue-green fungal layer on planted seeds, causing embryonic death or weak seedlings with pale green, stunted, and decaying leaves.
Small, circular to oval yellow spots on young leaf blades that lack a dark necrotic center, slowly expanding into wide yellow bands.
Small, irregular reddish-brown spots scattered across aging flag leaves, developing into dry, gray-centered lesions during hot, dry weather periods.
Irregular field patches of stunted, chlorotic plants; root systems are heavily restricted, showing an abundance of short, blunt, stubby root branches.
Brown, sunken, girdling lesions on young roots and coleoptiles, causing poorly filled patches in the field, leaf yellowing, and stunted development.
Water-soaked, slimy root disintegration in freshly germinated seeds; seedlings collapse right at the soil line or rot completely prior to emergence.
Water-soaked lesions on the upper third of glumes that dry into dark brown-black vertical stripes, occasionally leaking tiny white droplets under humid conditions.
Small, dark olive-green spots with fuzzy, velvety textures spreading across aging lower leaves, leading to localized yellowing and early leaf crisping.
Finely dashed green and bright yellow mosaic patterns appearing parallel to leaf veins, frequently followed by mild plant stunting and twisting of upper tips.
Reddish-brown to dark chocolate discoloration extending across the primary root lines, accompanied by poor tiller counts and small, bleached seed heads.
Dark purple-brown lens-shaped spots around leaf nodes and lower stem segments, structurally weakening the straw and causing it to snap under high winds.
Dull, dark gray-to-black rot covering the core crown area and primary roots, heavily speckled with microscopic black dots embedded directly into decayed skin tissue.
Dark charcoal-brown streaks creeping up the base of the main tillers, decaying the lower node centers and resulting in dead, silver-white heads at maturity.
Uneven field patches showing pale yellow leaves and poor growth; roots display tiny, branchy, localized swelling galls missing standard fine root hairs.
Dull gray or dark brown powdery mold staining the edges and grooves of developing kernels during humid weather, lowering seedling vigor scores.
Irregular, dry, papery tan spots forming on upper foliage, coated with flat clusters of deep black, glassy spores visible under magnification.
Fine, bright yellow-white continuous thread-like lines running cleanly along leaf edges, causing severe leaf curling and completely blind seed heads.
Reddish, orange, or wine-colored chalky stains appearing across outer kernel layers right at harvest, often overlapping with black point conditions.
Slow, stunted growth across large field areas; root networks display numerous tiny, distinct brown lesions, blunt tips, and general root hair loss.
A thick, white, fan-like fungal mat covering the stem base at the soil line, accompanied by small, round, light-brown survival structures resembling mustard seeds, causing sudden wilting.
Small, regular, dark brown oval spots on leaves that gradually develop lighter, straw-colored centers containing tiny, dark, embedded pimple-like structures.
Elongated, water-soaked, dark brown lesions on seedlings and lower foliage that coalesce into large, dead areas of leaf tissue, often covered in dark, olive-black velvety mold.
Deep, crater-like, sunken brown pits on the lower leaf sheaths and main crown nodes that physically disrupt the flow of plant nutrients and lead to lodging.
Oval or lens-shaped lesions on older leaves featuring distinct dark brown margins, tan-colored centers, and prominent light-green chlorotic borders or halos.
A powdery, jet-black accumulation of microscopic fungal spores clustering thickly along the central stem rachis and inner glume bases of prematurely bleached seed heads.
A characteristic yellow-to-brown discoloration starting on one side of the leaf blade, progressing down the vein line to induce premature leaf rolling and rapid plant death.
Dark brown to shiny black, water-soaked spots with highly irregular edges forming on lower leaves under wet conditions, drying out into a thin, brittle paper-like sheet.
A light pink, powdery, or dusty fungal layer coating the surfaces of individual wheat kernels within mature heads that have sustained heavy physical insect damage.
Fine, bright yellow, continuous parallel lines running the full length of the leaf surface, causing noticeable plant dwarfing and narrow leaf blade deformity.
Intense, vivid yellowing of leaf tips that slowly spreads downward to the leaf base, accompanied by a stiff, upright, bunched growth habit and reduced head size.
Patches of stunted, pale yellow plants displaying severe nutrient deficiency; roots are short, abnormally branched, and covered in small, hard, rounded swelling knots.
Individual grains inside the head are transformed into large, velvety, orange-yellow to dark green powdery spore balls that erupt through the glumes.
A black, crusty layer of fungal tissue surrounding and binding the leaf sheath tightly to the emerging head, completely arresting head expansion and grain development.
Thin, uniform field patches of sickly, yellowing plants with a severely stunted root architecture consisting of dark, shriveled root tips missing all root hairs.
Dark brown to black discoloration of the embryo end of the wheat kernel, spreading along the groove without shriveling the grain seed coat.
Dull yellow-green to dark blue-green powdery fungal patches forming across grain piles in bins, accompanied by musty odors and localized heating of grain.
Bright blue-green, velvet-like fungal colonies forming over damp or cracked grain coatings, rapidly destroying seed embryo viability and germination rates.
Pre-emergent decay of seeds or collapsing of young seedlings at the soil line, characterized by dark brown girdling lesions on tender root stems.
Eye-shaped structural lesions on the lowest leaf sheath near the soil surface, featuring dark borders and pale centers that cause fragile stems to break easily.
Elongated, water-soaked narrow stripes on leaves that turn yellowish-brown and translucent, forming brittle amber beads of dried bacterial ooze.
Narrow, pinkish-white lines of webbed fungal growth running vertically up leaf sheets during extended wet spring periods, causing leaf tips to wilt.
Stunted, thin, pale green plant development across field rows, with root systems showing microscopic brown scratches and dark necrotic lesion marks.
Extreme, uniform plant stunting, excessive weak tillering, and severe gold-yellow or red coloration of older leaf tips; transmitted by leafhoppers.
Severe yellow and light green mosaic mottling on leaves, accompanied by intense brown necrotic tearing of leaf tissue and stunted head development.
Discontinuous white, yellow, or light brown stripes forming a mosaic pattern on leaf surfaces, sometimes causing crinkling or severe splitting of leaf margins.
Lens-shaped brown lesions on leaves with dark borders and clear yellowish halos, featuring small, scattered, golden-brown embedded fruiting structures.
Olive-green to black velvet-like fuzzy mold layers growing across weathered, mature heads, often covering glumes without directly wrinkling internal grains.
Small orange, reddish-brown, or yellow speckles forming on aging leaves and glumes, which mature into dense, black powdery spots under humid weather.
Water-soaked rot at the base of the stem, producing dense cotton-white fungal mats that develop hard, charcoal-black survival bodies inside the straw center.
Elongated, bleach-colored lesions on leaves and sheaths containing tiny black hair-like structures (setae); premature ripening and washing out of stem brightness.
Small, oval, water-soaked brown spots on lower leaves that expand into large irregular necrotic lesions with concentric rings and dark margins.
Droplets of sticky, amber-colored honeydew liquid exuding from infected spikelets during flowering, prior to the formation of dark purplish ergot sclerotia spurs.
Extreme stunting of the plant (often one-half to one-fourth normal height), excessive tillering, and replacement of kernels with rounded smut balls containing dark, fishy-smelling spores.
Dark brown to purple-brown spots appearing first on glumes, later developing grayish centers covered with tiny, embedded black fruiting bodies (pycnidia).
Rapid yellowing and dying of lower leaves in large field patches during tillering; severe brown discolored rot on primary and secondary root tips.
Linear, light-green to yellow translucent streaks on leaves that become necrotic and brown; dried yellow flakes or beads of bacterial ooze on the leaf surface.
White-pink, crusty or slimy fungal mycelium mats covering dead, collapsed leaves right after winter snow melts; bleached crowns and root decay.
Severe twisting, curling, and distortion of the upper leaves and emerging seed heads, which are bound together by a black, crusty mass of fungal spores.
Premature bleaching of spikelets within the head, pink-to-orange spore masses at the base of glumes, and dark purplish-black perithecia forming on mature wheat heads.
Mild green to light yellow mosaic patterns, streaks, and dashes on leaf blades; slight reduction in plant vigor and overall seed count.
Bright yellow mosaic patches on leaves, often with necrotic brown tips; severe plant stunting and localized patch death across wet field zones.
Dark brown to black powdery spore masses replacing grain inside the spikelets; differs from loose smut by retaining a fragile covering membrane until maturity.
Stunted, pale-yellow patches of plants; root systems are short, excessively branched, and show a distinct 'bushy knots' appearance with tiny white cysts.
Swollen, twisted, distorted stems and leaf bases; shortened internodes giving plants a bunched 'dwarf-like' appearance; tissue becomes soft and rot-prone.
Dark brown to black necrotic lesions on the subcrown internode, crown, and roots; stunting, reduced tillering, and premature bleaching of individual tillers.
Chocolate-brown discoloration at the lower stem bases and leaf sheaths; pinkish-white fungal growth inside the stem or nodes under moist conditions; formation of whiteheads.
Lens-shaped lesions on lower leaf sheaths with sharply defined dark brown margins and pale straw-colored centers; weakens stems leading to lodging.
Distinct, continuous, bright yellow stripes running the full length of the leaf blade, with dark brown vascular strands visible within the stripes.
Slimy, water-soaked leaves covered in a web-like white to pinkish fungal mycelium appearing immediately after winter snow melt, causing leaf death.
Small, oval, water-soaked spots on leaves that rapidly turn brown and become surrounded by a prominent, wide, pale-yellow to green chlorotic halo.
Light green to yellow mosaic mottling and bright yellow flecking on young leaves; varying degrees of plant stunting occurring in distinct low-lying field patches.
Yellowish-green spindle-shaped streaks or dashes oriented parallel to the leaf veins; progresses to brown necrotic spots as older leaf tissue dies back.
Bright yellow, sticky, slimy bacterial slime or scum exuding across the emerging spikelet heads, twisting the heads and preventing grain formation; linked with nematode vectors.
General damping-off of seedlings; root systems exhibit a soft, water-soaked, yellowish-brown rot with complete loss of fine feeder root hairs.
Thickened, twisted, distorted, yellowing leaf structures; abnormal distortion of the seed head structure ('crazy top') where glumes morph into leaf-like extensions.
Distinct, circular patches of stunted, purple-tinted plants in the field; root systems within the patch are heavily pruned with brown, pointed 'needle-point' tips.
Eye-shaped lesions on the lower stem nodes near the soil line with a dark brown border and straw-colored center; central black dot may appear; causes lodging.
Large, irregular, pale gray to white bleached spots on leaves starting at the tip, filled with tiny submerged brown-black fruiting specs.
Long, narrow gray-black lines or blisters running parallel inside the leaf tissue; blisters rupture to expose an abundant dusty black mass of spores; leaves twist.
